Bambang has variable stress on some words, sometimes agreeing with Dupax, sometimes on the opposite syllable, e.g., Dupax /ʔánaʔ/, Bambang /ʔanáʔ/ ‘child’. Bambang appears to be losing contrast in lexical stress. In citation forms in Bambang, lexical stress is typically on the ultimate syllable, while in context, stress may sometimes appear on the penultimate syllable. Consequently, I do not mark stress on Bambang lexical forms in the examples in this paper.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is a phoneme of Isinay (Table 2). In the Dupax del Sur (and, per Reid 2020, phonologically near-identical Aritao) dialect, stress placement is lexically contrastive on disyllables: penult vs. ultima distinguishes words (gáyaŋ 'crow' / gayáŋ 'spear'); some analysts (Himes 1990; Reid & Salvador-Amores 2016) describe the same contrast as vowel length. In the Bambang dialect the contrast is being lost: citation forms are typically stressed on the final syllable, with penult stress appearing sometimes in connected speech. Scheerer 1918: 15 (Dupax-area data of a century earlier) gives the same picture from the other side: the majority of root words are penult-stressed (left unmarked), a minority are ultima-stressed (marked with an acute), and stress on the ultima varies in strength from word to word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialect split: Dupax del Sur keeps the lexical contrast; Bambang is variable, tending to final stress in citation forms and sometimes penult in context. Scheerer 1918: 15 fn. 1 notes final stress is very light in some words (ina, mata, batu) and very marked in derivatives (ataydn, orawdn); Scheerer's tables (pp. 16-20) show accent staying on the same syllable or shifting when -ar / possessive suffixes are added.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical forms and citation forms); Reid contrasts citation forms with forms 'in context' for Bambang. Scheerer's 'radical words' are roots in isolation, from a Dupax-area teacher.
new_statements.identity_note: Reid 2019 describes Isinay as three dialects: Dupax del Sur (with Aritao almost identical phonologically, Reid 2020: 2) and Bambang. The stress statement is dialect-split: Dupax del Sur/Aritao have lexically contrastive stress (or length), Bambang is losing it with citation-form final stress. Scheerer 1918 (data from a Dupax-area teacher, majority penult, minority ultima) agrees with the Dupax picture. No separate glottocodes exist for the dialects; all fall under isin1239.

sources.note: p. 15 (§11 preliminary remarks) + fn. 1: in the majority of radical words heard, the voice marks the penult; this common accent is left unmarked, the accented ultima is marked with an acute; stress on the ultima varies greatly in strength between words (very light in ina, mata, batu, very marked in derivatives like ataydn, orawdn); tables pp. 16-20 sort roots into 'penult accented' vs 'ultima accented' classes, i.e. lexically contrastive placement.
